# forge v0.11.0-rc.1 — a key of its own, a window of its own, and a second way to talk to Claude

A release candidate. It is the first build that changes how Forge reaches a
server, so **upgrading needs one manual step** — described at the bottom, and
shorter than it was going to be.

## Forge has a key of its own

```sh
forge setup
```

Makes this device an Ed25519 key, keeps it in `~/.forge`, and prints the line
that goes into a server's `authorized_keys`. Nothing else creates it — not a
first connection, not `host prepare` — because a key that appears as a side
effect is one nobody decided to trust.

Forge used to connect as *you*, borrowing whatever the machine already had: the
agent, or the first readable key in `~/.ssh`. That is a laptop's answer to a
question a phone cannot hear — there is no agent there, no `~/.ssh`, and no
`ssh-keygen` that ever ran. It also meant the same repository was pushed under
two identities depending on whether you or Claude ran the command.

The SSH client built in v0.10.0 and shipped switched off is now the default, and
it reads nothing of yours. `FORGE_SSH_BACKEND=exec` puts the `ssh` binary back
for one command, which is how you tell "is it the new client, or is it me".

## Chat

A second way into a workspace's Claude, beside the terminal. A prompt goes to the
same session and the answer streams back as it is written — the same binary, the
same login, no API key. The turn runs in tmux on the server, so it finishes
whether or not you are watching, and reloading the page brings the conversation
back rather than an empty box.

It exists because a phone cannot usefully render a TUI, and it is the mode that
will be there when Forge is an application.

## The preview

Alt-click a published port and it opens inside Forge, with an address bar,
instead of in another window. Several can be open at once, each with an entry in
the rail; the cross hides one and the trash ends it. On a narrow screen a port
opens here without asking — a tunnel lives in this application, so switching to a
browser takes it with you.

## A phone-shaped page

The layout gives way below 720px: the terminal and the shells go, the chat is the
mode, and the tree, ports and servers move off-canvas rather than away. It is the
same page — no second front end — and it is what the mobile app will show when
there is one.

## Servers answer for themselves

A host now records which workspaces are Forge's, which of its ports Forge may
hand out, and answers for both. That is what lets a second device see anything at
all: until now the list of workspaces lived in one laptop's config, so a phone
would have shown an empty Forge.

```sh
forge host adopt        # tell your servers what this device already knows
forge pair <public key> # let another device onto all of them
```

Pairing is three commands and no service in the middle: the new device says its
key, this one puts it on every server — the login *and* every workspace — and
hands back the list. A workspace deleted from one device now disappears from the
other, instead of being shown forever.

## Forge as an application

`Forge.app`, universal and signed, is attached to this release. It is the same
core in a window of its own: no browser tab, no daemon. Ad-hoc signed, so the
first open is right-click → Open.

## Smaller things

- Every server is asked at once rather than one after another. Four servers used
  to mean four handshakes end to end before anything on screen changed.
- Creating a workspace could leave an account behind that nothing claimed, which
  no later attempt could finish or delete. It resumes now.
- `forge workspace <name> ssh` no longer forwards your SSH agent — the browser's
  shell stopped in v0.10.0 and this one had not, so the same repository was pushed
  under two identities depending on which you opened.
- A page on a tunnelled port can no longer make Forge open terminals.

## Upgrading from v0.10.0

Your servers do not know this device's key yet, so the order matters.

**1. Install, without touching the servers yet:**

```sh
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Marb-AI/forge/main/install.sh \
  | FORGE_VERSION=v0.11.0-rc.1 FORGE_SKIP_AGENT_UPDATE=1 sh
```

**2. Make the key and copy the line it prints:**

```sh
forge setup
```

**3. Put that line on each server's login — from your own terminal, with your own
`ssh`, one last time.** This is the manual step, and the only one:

```sh
ssh <the target from `forge host list`>
mkdir -p ~/.ssh && touch ~/.ssh/authorized_keys
grep -qxF 'ssh-ed25519 AAAA…' ~/.ssh/authorized_keys || echo 'ssh-ed25519 AAAA…' >> ~/.ssh/authorized_keys
```

**4. Back on your machine, let Forge do the rest:**

```sh
forge host update                 # this build's agent
forge host adopt                  # which workspaces are Forge's, and its port range
forge pair "ssh-ed25519 AAAA…"    # the same line again: into every workspace too
forge forwarding start            # tunnels that failed to authenticate during the install
```

Step 4's `pair` is pairing this device with itself, which is exactly what it is:
a workspace's `authorized_keys` was written once, when it was created, with
whatever key that machine had then. Without it, the workspaces would list and
never open.

Then open the UI and check the things that use each login: a workspace shell and
a Claude session (workspace user), the host shell and the server metrics (admin
login), a tunnelled port, and the chat.

It being a release candidate: `FORGE_SSH_BACKEND=exec forge …` goes back to the
old behaviour for one command, and anything that needs it is worth reporting
rather than working around.
